blocks.x: You just took whatever was available. Yeah. Yeah. Then, uh, actually my big jump in learning tunes came when I was in Montana. When were you there? Well, first I served churches in Arkansas. No, wait, I'm sorry. It was in Louisiana when I became a member of the Baton Rouge Jazz Club. Oh, yes. And, uh, I used to play there. Uh, we had a meeting once a month and we used to, you know, listen to records for half the DA and then play for the rather half. And then I went from there to... Anybody in their band that, uh, got into professional work? In Baton Rouge group? In the Jazz Club of Baton Rouge. Well, we used to, they used to come in from New Orleans. One, uh, we had a jazz concert by George E. Gerard one evening before he died. And as I remember, Pete Fountain was in that band. He was here in Chicago and, uh, they played at Jazz Limited for a couple weeks while the Reinerks went on vacation. Oh. And, uh, Zimmerman was a piano player. Mm-hmm. I don't remember all the names. And, uh... I never had anything to do with them, but I knew the fellas who did. But the summer before we came here, uh, we were in Philadelphia and we went to see Louis Armstrong at a sort of a tent and around, you know, concert. And at intermission, my oldest child and I went back to get his autograph. And I asked him if he had ever... If they ever had any sessions after they were playing. And he said, oh, no, we're all tired. I said, I'd give my right arm to be able to play with you fellas. And, uh, he said, well, why don't you play right here? And there was about a thousand people out there. But I knew the opportunity would never come again. So I took him up for it. And this actually is what began this, uh, desire to be a pastor to some of these people. Well, then three weeks later, the Dukes arrived there called the Brandywine Music Tint. And, uh, this was in July, I guess it was, they arrived. And they said, well, if you play with Louis, you have to play with us. And then I was coming here. How did Brandywine spell? D-R-A-N-D-Y, W-I-N-E. Uh, we came here the first of September. The Dukes played the Butterfield Firehouse in October. And, uh, it was a Sunday night. And we were going to go out after youth group. And we were late. But they were later. They hadn't even started to play when we got there. And they started without a piano player. Their piano player got lost on the through way. So I walked up and they signaled me up and I played the whole first set. Well, of course, this was the beginning of the friendship, too, that has lasted. In fact, I played three times last week at Bourbon Street with them. And Sunday night I played with Art Hodes. Yeah. This helps the program, too. Yeah. When they introduce you with the new Knight Pastor on Rush Street. And, uh, this all helps. And Dave Remington has done this. And Bill Reinhardt have given me a tremendous boost in introducing them. Oh, that's good. Very good. Uh, well then... From that started, you know, some publicity in some of the newspapers. The press publications and the Trib, I think, did an article on me. And, uh, what we were trying to do. And how I used it. Could you accept a booking at any of those places along there for, uh, one appearance at nine o'clock? Play at an hour or something? Would I? Yeah. Uh, well I'd have to join the union. Let's see, you know, I was just thinking that, honey, that this card of yours doesn't belong. No, this doesn't mean anything. Uh, I know the union people pretty well. And maybe we could talk them into this as a, uh, uh, simply introducing you to Rush Street and, uh, they might also give you an honorary union card or something. Well, if you could work it, it'd be fine. If you'll tell me again how you happened to run into, uh, Louis Armstrong. And, uh, where was it that he invited you to play with me? Yeah, at the Brandywine Music tent. Brandywine Music tent. Which is right outside. Was that something that, uh, had existed in a while? No, it was a tent in the round bit. And they, the one summer they featured just, uh, musicians. And they'd booked them in for a week. Who else besides Louis played there? Oh, the Dukes. And, uh, um, there was a jazz trio at the time. Then, uh, man, two men and a girl. And they did a lot of singing. And then Count Basie's band was there for a week. Peter, Paul, and... No, no, no, this was, uh... Two men and women, I think. Land, Bert, Hendrickson. Oh, yes. And Ross. Oh, yes. A jazz group. Okay. Um, and, uh, you went to, uh, you went back to... We went to see Louis, and at intermission, Karen, my oldest child, wanted his autograph. So, I was in my collar. And, you know, the collar does get you into places at times. I don't try to take too much advantage of it, but I do every once in a while. So, we went right back, and I asked to see him. I was in, and I should write in. And I said, uh, this... I told him who I was, and I said, this is my daughter, Karen, and she wants your autograph. So he wrote to Karen, Satchmo. And then we started to talk, and I told him I played the piano. And I'd sure love to play with him. You know, just write it. Why don't you play with us here? Were you replacing Kyle? Yeah. Who else was in the band? Jeremy Young, and Billy Kyle, and, uh... Who else? Who was the clarinet band? Farney Begaard. And, uh... Who was on drums? Cozy? No, I don't think he was on drums. And that's Barrett? It might have been Cozy Cole. I don't know. I don't know. And, you know, he didn't even tell the band that I was going to do this. What was that? And then toward the end of the program, you know, I got a young fella here who likes to play the piano, plays a real fine piano. And, uh... We want to call him up. Let's see if we can get up. Father Owen, get up here. And the band, you know, they're looking at him like he's crazy, you know. And they look at me, you know. They shy away from me. And, uh... Of course, I was in a state of complete shock. You know, you dream about this. It's something you really dream about. And, uh... And Truman Young just couldn't take his... He couldn't walk away from the piano. It was real funny. Beverly said he just could not walk away from the piano. He didn't look, you know. And, uh... Then when I was all... I was all done, I just, you know, in complete shock, I said, Well, I can go home and die now. I just played with the king. And this broke them all up. But, you know, I was... From intermission until the time I played, I was just as white as a sheet. And... But I knew the opportunity would never come again. And it never has, really. I've seen him a few times. Talked with him. Visited with him. But I've never had an opportunity to play with him. He's coming, I understand, next month. Right about two days before our open house. And I'm wondering if he might go... Oh, maybe you can come in there and have a picture for the... For the walls in the archives. Yeah. Isn't that big enough? And, you know, Joe Glazer sent me $100 for this work. Is that so? Yeah. For the night pastry. For the night pastry. Good. Jeez, that's wonderful. And you said that in the same tent you played with the Dukes. Uh-huh. About three weeks later, they came in. And the fellow, more the publicity man for the tent. See, as soon as the thing was over, I left. With my family. Well, then he spent the next two or three days looking for me. You know, he couldn't figure out who I was and where I was and why I was.
